expectedText:
CALIFORNIA FAIR CHANCE ACT ('BAN THE BOX') — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Corp

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's Fair Chance Act (Government Code § 12952) — the state law restricting when and how Acme Corp may inquire about or consider the conviction history of an applicant for the position of Warehouse Associate, including Jordan Alex Lee, before and after making a conditional offer of employment. It states facts about what the statute itself requires and who it covers. This corpus separately includes a Background Check Adverse Action Notice — Information Sheet, which covers in more depth what happens once an employer has already made a conditional offer and is considering denying employment based on conviction history — the individualized assessment, the preliminary notice, the response window, and the final notice. This document focuses instead on the restriction that applies before that point: what an employer may and may not ask about, or consider, before a conditional offer is made, and which employers and positions the statute does or does not cover. It is not itself a job application, a conditional offer, an individualized assessment, or any notice, and it does not tell Acme Corp or Jordan Alex Lee what to do about any particular application, inquiry, or background-check result.

THE CORE PROHIBITION: NO INQUIRY BEFORE A CONDITIONAL OFFER
For a covered employer, California's Fair Chance Act makes it an unlawful employment practice to include any question seeking disclosure of an applicant's conviction history on a job application before a conditional offer of employment has been made, or to inquire into or consider an applicant's conviction history — including through any question on an employment application — at any point before a conditional offer of employment has been made. The statute states this obligation as applying to "an employer with five or more employees," subject to the exemptions described below.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) Except as provided in subdivision (d), it is an unlawful employment practice for an employer with five or more employees to do any of the following: (1) To include on any application for employment, before the employer makes a conditional offer of employment to the applicant, any question that seeks the disclosure of an applicant’s conviction history. (2) To inquire into or consider the conviction history of the applicant, including any inquiry about conviction history on any employment application, until after the employer has made a conditional offer of employment to the applicant."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(a)(1)-(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, pre-conditional-offer inquiry prohibition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12952.)
  Known gap: The statute doesn't itself define "conditional offer of employment." It also doesn't specify a required form for the offer (written, oral, or otherwise) or address what happens if an employer learns of conviction history involuntarily (for example, through a source other than its own inquiry) before making a conditional offer — this document does not address that scenario, which the statute's text doesn't speak to directly.

WHAT A CONVICTION HISTORY BACKGROUND CHECK MAY NOT CONSIDER
Separately from the timing restriction above, when a covered employer conducts a conviction history background check in connection with a job application, California law prohibits considering, distributing, or disseminating information about an arrest that was not followed by a conviction (with narrow statutory exceptions), a referral to or participation in a pretrial or posttrial diversion program, or a conviction that has been sealed, dismissed, expunged, or statutorily eradicated, or for which the person received a full pardon or a certificate of rehabilitation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(3) To consider, distribute, or disseminate information about any of the following while conducting a conviction history background check in connection with any application for employment: (A) Arrest not followed by conviction, except in the circumstances as permitted in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) and subdivision (f) of Section 432.7 of the Labor Code. (B) Referral to or participation in a pretrial or posttrial diversion program. (C) Convictions that have been sealed, dismissed, expunged, or statutorily eradicated pursuant to law, or any conviction for which the convicted person has received a full pardon or has been issued a certificate of rehabilitation."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, prohibited background-check content (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12952.)
  Known gap: The narrow exception referenced for non-conviction arrests cross-references Labor Code § 432.7, subdivisions (a)(1) and (f) — this document did not independently fetch and verify the text of Labor Code § 432.7 itself, so it states only that Government Code § 12952 makes this cross-reference, not what Section 432.7's exception itself covers in detail.

A BACKGROUND CHECK ITSELF IS NOT PROHIBITED
The Fair Chance Act does not itself prohibit a covered employer from conducting a conviction history background check on an applicant. What the statute restricts is the timing of any inquiry into conviction history (not before a conditional offer) and, separately, what the background check may consider, distribute, or disseminate, as described above.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(b) This section shall not be construed to prevent an employer from conducting a conviction history background check not in conflict with the provisions of subdivision (a)."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, background checks not otherwise prohibited (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12952.)
  Known gap: This clause states only what Government Code § 12952 itself says about background checks generally; it does not address the separate federal Fair Credit Reporting Act disclosure-and-authorization requirements that also apply to a background check performed through a third-party consumer reporting agency, which this corpus's Background Check Disclosure & Authorization document covers.

WHICH EMPLOYERS AND POSITIONS ARE COVERED OR EXEMPTED
California's Fair Chance Act, by its own terms, applies to "an employer with five or more employees." The statute lists four circumstances in which the section does not apply at all: a position for which a state or local agency is otherwise required by law to conduct a conviction history background check; a position with a criminal justice agency, as that term is defined in Penal Code § 13101; a position as a Farm Labor Contractor, as described in Labor Code § 1685; and a position where the employer or its agent is required by state, federal, or local law to conduct criminal background checks for employment purposes or to restrict employment based on criminal history — a category the statute says includes rules or regulations issued by a self-regulatory organization under the federal Securities Exchange Act of 1934.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(d) This section does not apply in any of the following circumstances: (1) To a position for which a state or local agency is otherwise required by law to conduct a conviction history background check. (2) To a position with a criminal justice agency, as defined in Section 13101 of the Penal Code. (3) To a position as a Farm Labor Contractor, as described in Section 1685 of the Labor Code. (4) To a position where an employer or agent thereof is required by any state, federal, or local law to conduct criminal background checks for employment purposes or to restrict employment based on criminal history."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(d)(1)-(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, statutory exemptions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12952.)
  "For purposes of this paragraph, federal law shall include rules or regulations promulgated by a self-regulatory organization as defined in Section 3(a)(26) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended by 124 Stat. 1652 (Public Law 111-203), pursuant to the authority in Section 19(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended by 124 Stat. 1652 (Public Law 111-203)."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(d)(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, self-regulatory-organization clause within the fourth exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12952.)
  Known gap: This clause catalogs the exemptions that the corpus's existing Background Check Adverse Action Notice — Information Sheet document flagged but did not itself list (that document's gap field noted the five-or-more-employee threshold is "subject to statutory exceptions... that this document doesn't catalog"). The statute doesn't define "employee" for purposes of counting toward the five-employee threshold (for example, whether part-time, out-of-state, or temporary staffing employees count), and this document doesn't resolve that question.

HOW THE STATUTE DEFINES "CONVICTION" AND "CONVICTION HISTORY"
For purposes of the Fair Chance Act, "conviction" carries the same meaning given to it in Labor Code § 432.7(a)(1) and (a)(3). The broader term "conviction history" is defined to also include an arrest not resulting in conviction, but only in the specific, limited circumstance described in Labor Code § 432.7(f), where an employer at a health facility (as defined in Health and Safety Code § 1250) may ask an applicant for certain positions about specified types of arrests, and an arrest for which a person is out on bail or on their own recognizance pending trial.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(f) For purposes of this section: (1) “Conviction” has the same meaning as defined in paragraphs (1) and (3) of subdivision (a) of Section 432.7 of the Labor Code. (2) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), the term “conviction history” includes: (A) An arrest not resulting in conviction only in the specific, limited circumstances described in subdivision (f) of Section 432.7 of the Labor Code, when an employer at a health facility, as defined in Section 1250 of the Health and Safety Code, may ask an applicant for certain positions about specified types of arrests. (B) An arrest for which an individual is out on bail or his or her own recognizance pending trial."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(f) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, definitions of "conviction" and "conviction history" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12952.)
  Known gap: This document verified only the definitional text of Government Code § 12952(f) itself, which cross-references Labor Code § 432.7 for both the core definition of "conviction" and the health-facility arrest exception; it did not independently fetch and verify the text of Labor Code § 432.7, so it does not state what that section's own definitions or the health-facility exception specifically cover beyond what § 12952(f) itself says about them.

AFTER A CONDITIONAL OFFER: THE INDIVIDUALIZED-ASSESSMENT PROCESS APPLIES
The pre-offer inquiry restriction described above is not the end of the Fair Chance Act's protection. The same statute goes on to require, once a covered employer has made a conditional offer and is considering denying employment based on conviction history, an individualized assessment, a written preliminary notice with a right to respond, and — if a final decision to deny is made — a written final notice. The statute also requires the employer to consider any information the applicant submits in response to the preliminary notice before making that final decision.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(4) The employer shall consider information submitted by the applicant pursuant to paragraph (3) before making a final decision."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(c)(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, employer must consider applicant's response before a final decision (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12952.)
  Known gap: This corpus's Background Check Adverse Action Notice — Information Sheet document independently verifies and quotes the individualized-assessment factors, the required content of the preliminary and final notices, and the business-day response window (Gov. Code § 12952(c)(1)-(3) and (c)(5)); this clause does not restate those quotes. It instead verifies and quotes only paragraph (c)(4) — the requirement that the employer consider the applicant's submitted response before finalizing a decision — which that other document does not separately quote, so that this document's own overview of the full pre-offer-to-final-decision timeline rests on independently verified text rather than an unverified summary of the other document's content.

SIGNATURE AND CERTIFICATION

Position applied for: Warehouse Associate
Date: _______________

Acme Corp certifies that this information sheet was provided to Jordan Alex Lee.

Company representative: _______________
